title: Endocrine Tumour Markers: Metanephrines, Calcitonin, Macroprolactin and the Hook Effect
summary: Learn why plasma free metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma, how calcitonin detects medullary thyroid cancer and why its cut-offs vary, and why a pituitary mass with an abnormal prolactin needs thyroid testing, macroprolactin screening and dilution for the hook effect.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 25 Hit 2 (plasma free metanephrines), Hit 10 (macroprolactinemia and the high-dose hook effect), Hit 12 (calcitonin as the MTC marker) and Exam Trap 3 (hyperprolactinemia plus pituitary mass). Checked against Eisenhofer 2022, Rao 2017 and the Japan Endocrine Society 2025 PPGL guideline (Tanabe 2026); Broecker-Preuss 2023, Trimboli 2024, Fugazzola 2021 and Kim 2021 for calcitonin and MTC; Kasum 2012, Shimatsu 2012, Fukuhara 2022, Khan 2025, Agarwal 2010 and Gonçalves 2023 for prolactin; all read as Europe PMC full text. The 2015 ATA MTC guideline (Wells 2015) returned no full text from Europe PMC and was not read; the Endocrine Society PPGL and hyperprolactinemia guidelines were not read. Not taught: the reviewer’s metanephrine values (<112/>400 ng/L normetanephrine, <61/>236 ng/L metanephrine; register flag rv-metanephrine-fixed-cutoffs), the basal calcitonin cut-offs 18.7/68 pg/mL as fixed values (register flag rv-calcitonin-basal-cutoffs) and the pentagastrin >100 ng/L = C-cell hyperplasia rule (register flag rv-calcitonin-pentagastrin-cch). The reviewer’s “one-site assays” wording for the hook effect is replaced by one-step sandwich (two-antibody) assays (register flag rv-prolactin-hook-one-site).

objectives: Explain why plasma free metanephrines are a more sensitive screen for pheochromocytoma than catecholamines, and list the sampling conditions that limit false positives.

Interpret calcitonin as the marker of medullary thyroid cancer, including sex- and assay-specific cut-offs, non-tumour causes of a raised value and the need to exclude pheochromocytoma before surgery.
Work up hyperprolactinemia with a pituitary mass: thyroid function, macroprolactin by PEG precipitation, stalk compression, and dilution for the high-dose hook effect.

scenes.title: Three tumour suspects
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three adults. (1) Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with a 3 cm adrenal mass; plasma free normetanephrine is 3 times the upper cut-off. (2) A thyroid nodule with an elevated basal calcitonin; the RET gene status is unknown and surgery is being planned. (3) A 4.6 cm sellar mass with visual field loss; prolactin is only 42 ng/mL. Question token: “Which marker do you trust, and what must happen next?”

cues.text: Three patients. The first has spells of headache, sweating and palpitations, an adrenal mass, and a plasma normetanephrine three times the upper cut-off.
The second has a thyroid nodule with a high calcitonin, and surgery is being planned. The third has a huge pituitary mass but a prolactin of only forty-two.
Which marker can you trust, and what has to happen before anyone acts on it?

props.label: Which marker do you trust, and what next?

scenes.title: Where the markers come from
scenes.altText: Schematic source cards. Chromaffin cells: catecholamines are metabolised inside the same cells by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), a continuous process that runs independently of secretion, giving metanephrine and normetanephrine. Thyroid C (parafollicular) cells: secrete calcitonin; serum calcitonin and CEA track C-cell mass. Lactotrophs: prolactin is tonically suppressed by hypothalamic dopamine; TRH and oestrogen stimulate it. Forms card: monomeric (little) prolactin about 23 kDa, big prolactin a dimer, and big-big prolactin (macroprolactin, above about 100–150 kDa), mostly prolactin bound to IgG autoantibody.

cues.text: In the adrenal medulla, catecholamines are broken down inside the same chromaffin cells by the enzyme COMT. This runs continuously, whether or not the cell is secreting, and gives metanephrine and normetanephrine.
In the thyroid, the C cells, also called parafollicular cells, make calcitonin. Serum calcitonin, along with CEA, rises with the mass of C cells.
In the pituitary, lactotrophs are held back by dopamine from the hypothalamus, and are stimulated by TRH and oestrogen.
Most prolactin in blood is a small monomer of about twenty-three kilodaltons. Macroprolactin is a much larger complex, mostly prolactin bound to an IgG autoantibody.

scenes.title: What each tumour does to its marker
scenes.altText: Three tumour cards. Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL): tumour secretion of catecholamines can be intermittent, but intratumoral O-methylation is continuous, so plasma free metanephrines outperform catecholamines and VMA (sensitivity about 97–99% vs 46–77% for VMA in adults, per Eisenhofer 2022). Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC): calcitonin is the most reliable test to detect it; about 1 in 4 cases is inherited (familial MTC or MEN2 with RET mutations). Prolactinoma: tumour volume usually correlates with prolactin. Mimic card: stalk or hypothalamic masses reduce dopamine inhibition; primary hypothyroidism raises TRH, which raises prolactin and can enlarge the pituitary (hyperplasia that looks like an adenoma and regresses on levothyroxine); macroprolactin raises measured prolactin through slow clearance, not more secretion.

cues.text: A pheochromocytoma may release catecholamines in bursts, but it makes metanephrines all the time. That is why plasma free metanephrines catch about ninety-seven to ninety-nine percent of these tumours in adults, far more than the older VMA test.
In medullary thyroid cancer, calcitonin is the most reliable test for detection. About one in four cases is inherited, as familial disease or multiple endocrine neoplasia type two.
In a prolactinoma, the prolactin level usually rises with the size of the tumour. But a pituitary mass with a raised prolactin is not always a prolactinoma.

A mass pressing on the stalk blocks dopamine. Primary hypothyroidism raises TRH, which raises prolactin and can even enlarge the pituitary. And macroprolactin raises the number only because it is cleared slowly.

scenes.title: Getting the number right
scenes.altText: Workflow cards. Metanephrines: sample after at least 20 minutes supine through an indwelling cannula; upper cut-offs are method- and age-specific (one LC-MS/MS study: normetanephrine about 100–200 pg/mL rising with age, metanephrine 88 pg/mL); positive results for two or more metabolites or rises of 2-fold or more above cut-offs indicate close to 100% probability of tumour. Calcitonin: sex-specific reference ranges (men have about twice as many C cells); no consensus basal cut-off, values from published studies range from about 18.7 to 35 pg/mL in women and 34 to 68 pg/mL in men; non-tumour rises with chronic kidney disease, proton pump inhibitors, smoking and C-cell hyperplasia; pentagastrin has been unavailable since about 2010–2011, calcium stimulation is the alternative but debated; exclude pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines) and hyperparathyroidism before MTC surgery when RET status is unknown or positive. Prolactin: PEG precipitation, recovery below about 40% (thresholds vary <30–50%) indicates macroprolactin; gel filtration is the reference method; large tumours with modest prolactin need diluted re-assay for the hook effect. Hook answers.

cues.text: Metanephrines: sample after at least twenty minutes lying down, through a cannula. Cut-offs depend on the method and the patient’s age. Rises of two-fold or more, or several metabolites high together, make a tumour close to certain.

Calcitonin: use sex-specific limits, because men have about twice as many C cells. There is no agreed single cut-off, and kidney disease, proton pump inhibitors and smoking can raise it. Pentagastrin testing is no longer available.
Prolactin: treat the serum with polyethylene glycol. If less than about forty percent is recovered, macroprolactin is present. With a large tumour and a modest prolactin, re-run the sample diluted.
Back to the hook. Patient one has a near-certain tumour and goes to imaging. Patient two needs metanephrines and calcium checked before thyroid surgery. Patient three needs a diluted prolactin.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Pituitary mass + high prolactin = prolactinoma” (✓ check TSH, macroprolactin and stalk compression first); “A normal prolactin rules out prolactinoma in a giant adenoma” (✓ hook effect: re-assay on dilution); “Calcitonin confirms MTC, so go straight to thyroidectomy” (✓ exclude pheochromocytoma first when RET status is unknown or positive).

cues.text: Trap one: a pituitary mass plus a high prolactin means prolactinoma. No: check thyroid function, screen for macroprolactin, and remember stalk compression.
Trap two: a normal prolactin rules out a prolactinoma in a giant adenoma. No: the hook effect can make it read falsely low, so re-run it diluted.
Trap three: a high calcitonin means straight to thyroid surgery. No: if the RET status is unknown or positive, rule out a pheochromocytoma first.

props.title: ✗ “Normal prolactin rules it out.”
lines: ✓ Giant adenoma: dilute for the hook effect

scenes.title: Fingerprints, headcount, heavy ghost
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Metanephrines are FINGERPRINTS the tumour leaves all the time, even when the catecholamine burglar is quiet. Calcitonin is a C-cell HEADCOUNT. Macroprolactin is a HEAVY GHOST: big, slow to leave and mostly harmless. The hook effect is a CROWDED DOOR: too much prolactin jams the antibodies, so dilute the crowd.” Tokens: fingerprints = metanephrines · headcount = calcitonin · heavy ghost = macroprolactin · crowded door = hook. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: metanephrines are fingerprints left all the time, even when the burglar is quiet. Calcitonin is a headcount of C cells. Macroprolactin is a heavy ghost, big and slow to leave. And the hook effect is a crowded door: dilute the crowd.

Where it breaks: metanephrines also rise with stress, upright sampling and some drugs; calcitonin rises in kidney disease, with proton pump inhibitors and in C-cell hyperplasia; macroprolactin can coexist with true high prolactin; and the hook effect depends on the assay.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Macroprolactin can coexist with true excess

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Pheochromocytoma → plasma free metanephrines, sampled supine”, “Medullary thyroid cancer → calcitonin, sex- and assay-specific; exclude pheochromocytoma before surgery”, “Pituitary mass + prolactin → TSH, PEG for macroprolactin, dilute for the hook effect”.

cues.text: Trust plasma free metanephrines for pheochromocytoma and calcitonin for medullary thyroid cancer only when they are sampled and interpreted correctly, and never call a pituitary mass a prolactinoma until thyroid function, macroprolactin and the hook effect have been checked.

props.label: Pheo → plasma free metanephrines, supine sampling
MTC → calcitonin (sex/assay-specific); exclude pheo before surgery

explanation.what: Plain language: some endocrine tumours are found through a substance they release into blood. An adrenal pheochromocytoma leaves breakdown products of adrenaline-type hormones, a thyroid C-cell cancer releases calcitonin, and a pituitary prolactinoma releases prolactin. Each marker has a classic way of misleading you. Scientific terms: pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), catecholamines, catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), plasma free metanephrine and normetanephrine, methoxytyramine, vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), C (parafollicular) cells, calcitonin, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), C-cell hyperplasia (CCH), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), RET, lactotroph, dopamine, thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), macroprolactin (big-big prolactin), polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation, gel filtration chromatography, high-dose hook effect.
explanation.why: PPGLs express COMT and convert catecholamines to metanephrines continuously inside tumour cells, while catecholamine release can be intermittent, so metanephrines give a steadier signal. Calcitonin output rises with C-cell mass, so it detects MTC; men have about twice the C-cell density of women. Prolactin is tonically inhibited by dopamine, so stalk compression raises it; TRH stimulates it, so primary hypothyroidism raises it; macroprolactin (prolactin bound to IgG autoantibody) is cleared slowly and has low bioactivity in vivo. In a one-step sandwich immunoassay, extreme prolactin excess saturates both antibodies so few sandwiches form, giving a falsely low result.
explanation.measure: Plasma free metanephrines: blood drawn through a cannula after at least 20 minutes supine; age- and method-specific upper cut-offs (one LC-MS/MS study: normetanephrine about 100–200 pg/mL rising with age; metanephrine 88 pg/mL); rises of 2-fold or more above cut-offs, or two or more metabolites positive, indicate close to 100% probability. Calcitonin: sex-specific reference ranges; published basal cut-offs vary (about 18.7–35 pg/mL women, 34–68 pg/mL men; Fugazzola 2021: >30 women, >34 men); proposed grey zones 20–30 pg/mL (women) and 30–60 pg/mL (men); preoperative >500 pg/mL suggests metastases; pentagastrin unavailable since about 2010–2011; calcium-stimulated calcitonin is debated. Prolactin: PEG precipitation, recovery below about 40% (thresholds <30–50%) indicates macroprolactin, with PEG-specific reference intervals for the monomer; gel filtration chromatography is the reference; dilute samples from patients with large tumours and modest prolactin.
explanation.differs: Metanephrines (continuous intratumoral metabolites; high sensitivity) vs catecholamines and VMA (episodic, diluted by other sources; lower sensitivity). MTC (calcitonin rises with tumour size; CEA often raised) vs non-tumour hypercalcitoninemia (CKD, proton pump inhibitors, smoking, C-cell hyperplasia). Prolactinoma (prolactin tracks tumour size; true monomeric excess) vs macroprolactinemia (inactive complexes, often no symptoms) vs stalk effect or hypothyroidism (secondary rise) vs hook effect (falsely low reading with a giant tumour).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose plasma free metanephrines as the most sensitive pheochromocytoma screen and pick the sampling condition that avoids false positives; recognise calcitonin as the MTC marker and test for pheochromocytoma before thyroidectomy; spot macroprolactin from an asymptomatic patient with low PEG recovery; choose dilution when a giant pituitary mass has a normal or mildly raised prolactin; check TSH in hyperprolactinemia.

left.label: Plasma free metanephrines
points: Made continuously inside tumour cells by COMT

right.label: Catecholamines / VMA
points: Released episodically; VMA diluted by other sources

left.label: MTC
points: Often keeps rising on follow-up; CEA may be raised

Usually mild and stable or falling

Low PEG recovery; often no symptoms

points: Giant tumour; rises sharply on dilution

mnemonic.text: Metanephrines are FINGERPRINTS the tumour leaves all the time, even when the catecholamine burglar is quiet. Calcitonin is a C-cell HEADCOUNT. Macroprolactin is a HEAVY GHOST: big, slow to leave and mostly harmless. The hook effect is a CROWDED DOOR: too much prolactin jams the antibodies, so dilute the crowd.
mnemonic.explanation: Links each marker to the reason it works (continuous metabolites, C-cell mass) or misleads (large inactive complexes, antibody saturation).
mnemonic.limitation: Metanephrines also rise with stress, upright or venipuncture sampling and some drugs; calcitonin also rises with chronic kidney disease, proton pump inhibitors, smoking and C-cell hyperplasia; macroprolactin can coexist with true monomeric hyperprolactinemia and some macroprolactinemic patients have symptoms; the hook effect depends on the assay and is rarely seen in some chemiluminescent systems.

analogyLimitations: Cell and assay drawings are schematic.
The burglar, ghost and door images ignore drug effects and assay differences that change real cut-offs.
takeaway: Trust plasma free metanephrines for pheochromocytoma and calcitonin for medullary thyroid cancer only when they are sampled and interpreted correctly, and never call a pituitary mass a prolactinoma until thyroid function, macroprolactin and the hook effect have been checked.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has bitemporal visual field loss and a 4.6 cm invasive sellar mass. Serum prolactin on a one-step sandwich immunoassay is 42 ng/mL. TSH and free T4 are normal. What should the laboratory do next?

options.text: Repeat prolactin on a diluted sample
options.rationale: Correct. A giant tumour with only a modest prolactin suggests the high-dose hook effect; dilution lets the true, much higher value appear.

options.text: Report a stalk effect from a non-functioning adenoma
options.rationale: Incorrect. Stalk compression can explain a modest rise, but in a giant tumour the hook effect must be excluded first by dilution.
Incorrect. Macroprolactin makes prolactin look falsely high; it cannot explain a falsely low value in a giant tumour.
Incorrect. Metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma, not for a pituitary mass.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with regular menses and no galactorrhoea has prolactin 85 ng/mL on two occasions. TSH is normal and she takes no medicines. After PEG precipitation, recovery is 22% and the post-PEG prolactin is within the PEG-specific reference interval. Best interpretation?

options.text: Macroprolactinemia: most of the prolactin is big inactive complexes
options.rationale: Correct. Recovery well below about 40% with a normal monomeric prolactin indicates macroprolactin, which usually needs no imaging or dopamine agonist.
Incorrect. The monomeric (active) prolactin is normal, so there is no true hyperprolactinemia to treat.

options.text: High-dose hook effect: dilute and repeat
options.rationale: Incorrect. The hook effect gives falsely low values with very high prolactin, usually in giant tumours; it does not cause low PEG recovery.

options.text: Primary hypothyroidism causing TRH-driven prolactin release
options.rationale: Incorrect. TSH is normal, which argues against primary hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old has a thyroid nodule, basal calcitonin 420 pg/mL and fine-needle aspiration consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma. Germline RET status is not yet known. Which test should be done before thyroidectomy?

options.text: Plasma free (fractionated) metanephrines, with serum calcium
options.rationale: Correct. With unknown or positive RET status, pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism must be excluded; a pheochromocytoma is removed first to avoid a hypertensive crisis during surgery.
Incorrect. The diagnosis is already established, and pentagastrin has not been available for this use since about 2010–2011.

options.text: None: the calcitonin already confirms the diagnosis, so proceed to surgery
options.rationale: Incorrect. Calcitonin supports MTC but says nothing about a coexisting pheochromocytoma, which must be excluded first when RET status is unknown.
Incorrect. Macro-forms are a pitfall for mild calcitonin rises; they do not change the need to exclude pheochromocytoma before surgery.

claims.text: Catecholamines are metabolised to metanephrines by COMT inside chromaffin and PPGL cells continuously and independently of secretion; catecholamine release can be intermittent.
Plasma free metanephrines have sensitivity about 97–99% in adults vs 46–77% for VMA; metanephrines are recommended over catecholamines.

Sampling after at least 20 minutes supine through a cannula reduces false positives; cut-offs are age- and method-specific; 2-fold rises or two or more positive metabolites indicate close to 100% probability.
Calcitonin is produced by thyroid C cells and is the most reliable test to detect MTC; calcitonin and CEA track C-cell mass; about 1 in 4 MTC is inherited (MEN2/familial, RET).

Calcitonin reference ranges are sex-specific (men about twice the C-cell density); there is no consensus basal cut-off and published cut-offs range about 18.7–35 pg/mL (women) and 34–68 pg/mL (men); CKD, proton pump inhibitors and smoking cause non-specific rises.
Pentagastrin has been unavailable since about 2010–2011; the calcium stimulation test is the alternative but its value is debated.
With unknown or positive germline RET status, exclude pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines) and hyperparathyroidism (calcium) before thyroid surgery; a pheochromocytoma is removed first.
claims.note: Kim 2021 summarises ATA 2015, ESMO and NCCN guidance; the ATA 2015 guideline itself was not read.

claims.text: Prolactin is tonically suppressed by dopamine and stimulated by TRH and oestrogen; stalk/hypothalamic masses and primary hypothyroidism raise prolactin; hypothyroid pituitary hyperplasia can mimic adenoma and regresses on thyroid hormone.

Macroprolactin is mainly prolactin–IgG complex (>100–150 kDa) with low in-vivo bioactivity and slow clearance; detected by PEG precipitation (recovery <~40%, thresholds vary) with gel filtration as reference; often asymptomatic but can coexist with true monomeric excess.
In giant prolactinomas, antibody saturation in sandwich immunoassays can give falsely low prolactin (high-dose hook effect); re-assay on dilution; prolactin usually correlates with tumour size.

Reviewer: normetanephrine <112 / >400 ng/L and metanephrine <61 / >236 ng/L as rule-out/rule-in values; basal calcitonin 18.7 (women) / 68 (men) pg/mL as fixed cut-offs; pentagastrin (0.5 μg/kg) calcitonin >100 ng/L = C-cell hyperplasia.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 25 Hit 2 (and the Number Vault) gives normetanephrine >400 ng/L and metanephrine >236 ng/L as “very high probability” values (rule-out <112 / <61 ng/L). No source read gives these values. Rao 2017 (LC-MS/MS, supine sampling) uses age-specific normetanephrine cut-offs of about 100–200 pg/mL and metanephrine 88 pg/mL, and judges probability by fold-increase above the cut-off and number of positive metabolites. The lesson teaches method- and age-specific cut-offs and the fold-increase rule (register flag rv-metanephrine-fixed-cutoffs).

Ch. 25 Hit 12 gives basal calcitonin cut-offs of 18.7 pg/mL (women) and 68 pg/mL (men) as if fixed. Broecker-Preuss 2023 shows these are the extremes of published study cut-offs (>18.7 to ≥35 pg/mL women, >34 to >68 pg/mL men), Fugazzola 2021 derives >30/>34 pg/mL, and Trimboli 2024 states there is no consensus cut-off and that assays differ (register flag rv-calcitonin-basal-cutoffs).

Ch. 25 Hit 12 says pentagastrin stimulation (0.5 μg/kg) with calcitonin >100 ng/L = C-cell hyperplasia. Broecker-Preuss 2023 reports that pentagastrin has not been approved or available since 2010/2011 (calcium gluconate stimulation replaced it, with debated value) and describes stimulated calcitonin >100 pg/mL as the threshold at which MTC risk is substantial and thyroidectomy is warranted, not as a C-cell hyperplasia criterion; C-cell hyperplasia and MTC overlap (register flag rv-calcitonin-pentagastrin-cch).

Ch. 25 Hit 10 says giant prolactinomas read falsely low on “one-site assays”. Sources read describe the hook effect as saturation of the assay antibodies in sandwich (two-antibody) immunoassays (Agarwal 2010, Fukuhara 2022), and the reviewer’s own Memory Hook says one-step sandwich assays. The lesson uses the sandwich wording (register flag rv-prolactin-hook-one-site).
